Independently of the work in [11], Jurrius and Pellikaan [9] defined the derived code of a linear code. This work was then not noticed by Oxley and Wang [14]. Both constructions give a derived matroid for a representable matroid, and we will see that the definitions are dual to each other. The main difference is thus that the following definition from [9] uses the cocircuits as the ground set for the derived code. The construction is based on the construction of a derived hyperplane arrangement given in [5, §5.10].
Definition 3.4 ([9], Definition 4.1).
Let G be a k×n matrix of rank k over a field 𝔽. Let J⊆{1,…,n}. Let 𝐠j be the j-th column of G. Let GJ be the k×|J| submatrix of G consisting of the columns 𝐠j with j in J. Let GJ​(X) be the k×(|J|+1) matrix obtained by adding the column X=(X1,…,Xk)T to GJ, where X1,…,Xk are variables. Let Gi,J be the (k−1)×|J| matrix obtained by deleting the i-th row of GJ. Let ΔJ​(X)=det(GJ​(X)) and Δi,J=det(Gi,J) in case |J|=k−1. Let D⁡(G) be the derived matrix of G of size k×(nk−1) with entries Δi,J with i=1,…,k and J⊆{1,…,n} of size k−1 ordered lexicographically. The matrix D2​(G) is obtained by removing zero columns and columns that are a scalar multiple of another column. The derived code D2​(C) is the code with generator matrix D2​(G).
It was shown in [9] that the construction of D2​(C) is independent of the choice of generator matrix G.
Geometrically, D2​(G) is constructed as follows. For every subset of k−1 columns of G, check if they are independent in 𝔽k. If not, add a zero column to D⁡(G). If they are independent, take the coefficients of a linear form determining this (k−1)-space and make them into a column of D⁡(G). Then remove zeros and multiple subsets that span the same (k−1)-space.
From this geometric interpretation, one can see that this construction is the same as δO​W of the dual matroid. Every set of k−1 columns of G (i.e., elements of M) that has rank k−1 contributes to a column in D⁡(G). If another set of k−1 columns spans the same (k−1)-space, the corresponding column in D⁡(G) will be removed from D2​(G). Hence all the columns of D2​(G) correspond to a hyperplane of the matroid represented by G. Since there is a one-to-one correspondence between hyperplanes of M and circuits of M∗, this gives the desired duality relation. Note that in the construction of δO​W one gets a representation that is not of full rank, whereas the definition of D2​(G) does, by definition, give a full rank matrix.
3.4 Adjoint matroid

The map ψ:L→LΔ has the following properties:

The construction of the derived code by Jurrius and Pellikaan gives in fact an adjoint: the map ψ defined in [9, Definition 4.15] satisfies the properties of the map ψ in Definition 3.5.
4 Construction of the combinatorial derived matroid
We are now ready to present our definition of the combinatorial derived matroid δ​M of a matroid M with circuit set 𝒞. In fact, we will make two such definitions, one of which defines the circuits and the other of which defines the dependent sets of δ​M. The definitions are very similar, but a priori different, and we will introduce them both before we prove that they indeed yield the same matroid.
For motivation, we first assume that M is represented by some code Q over a field 𝔽. Like in Section 3.2, for each set S of M we define
Q⟂​(S)={q∈Q⟂:supp⁡(q)⊆S},
and for each circuit C of M we let qC be a vector in Q⟂ with supp⁡(qC)=C, noting that qC is unique up to scalar multiple.
For any collection A⊆𝒞 of circuits, we have
span{qC:C∈A}⊆Q⟂(∪C∈AC),
where span denotes the linear span over 𝔽. Hence, if
dim(Q⟂(∪C∈AC))<|A|,
(1)
then the dual codewords qC:C∈A are linearly dependent regardless of the chosen representation Q, and so we would like them to be dependent in the combinatorial derived matroid.
Now by standard duality arguments,
Q⟂​(S)=(Q|S)⟂,
where Q|S is the projection of Q to the coordinates in S. Thus
dim(Q⟂​(S))=|S|−dim(Q|S)=n⁡(S),
so the condition (1), which is sufficient for dependence of {qC:C∈A} can be rewritten as
n(∪C∈AC)<|A|.
(2)

Moreover, we define

The operation ϵ:2𝒞→2𝒞 is designed to guarantee properties (C3) and (D3) in the matroid axioms.
Definition 4.2.
Let M be a matroid, and 𝒞=𝒞⁡(M) its collection of circuits. Define the collection
𝒜0:={A⊆𝒞:|A|>n(∪C∈AC)}.
(3)
Inductively, we let 𝒜i+1=↑ϵ⁡(𝒜i) for i≥1, and
𝒜=⋃i≥0𝒜i.
Analogously, we let ℬ0=min⁡𝒜0, ℬi+1=ϵ⁡(ℬi) for i≥1, and
ℬ=min⋃i≥0ℬi.
For a set A∈𝒜i+1∖𝒜i, respectively B∈ℬi+1∖ℬi, we say that it has depth i+1 in 𝒜 or ℬ respectively.
Note that the sequences 𝒜i and ℬi are both increasing and contained in the finite set 2𝒞. Hence, we have that 𝒜0⊆𝒜 and 𝒜=𝒜n for some n≥0, and analogously ℬ0⊆ℬ and ℬ=ℬn for some n≥0.
Definition 4.3.
Let M be a matroid with circuits 𝒞. Then the combinatorial derived matroid δ​M is a matroid with ground set 𝒞⁡(M) and dependent sets 𝒜. Alternatively, we can define δ​M by its circuits ℬ.
We will prove, in Propositions 4.7 and 4.9, that these definitions gives indeed a matroid and that the two definitions are the same. After this, we will define yet another way to construct the circuit set ℬ, in Proposition 4.10.
Remark 4.4.
Rewriting axiom (D3) in the logically equivalent form:
if ​D1,D2∈𝒟,
then ​D1∩D2∈𝒟​ or ​(D1∪D2)∖{e}∈𝒟​ for all ​e∈D1∩D2,
we could in principle for every A1,A2∈𝒜i such that A1∩A2∉𝒜i, have chosen to include either A1∩A2 or (A1∪A2)∖{C} into 𝒜i+1. By defining 𝒜i+1 via the operation ϵ, as in Definition 4.2, we guarantee to not construct any small dependent sets when not necessary. This appears as a desirable property for the constructed derived matroid to be “generic”.
Indeed, consequently choosing to include D1∩D2 in 𝒜 for all prescribed dependent sets D1,D2∈𝒜 would result in a rather less interesting matroid — often even with rank 0.

Corollary 5.4.
Let M=U⁡(k,n) be a uniform matroid with k≥n−3. Then δ​M=(𝒞,𝒜0).
Proof.
We will show that 𝒜0 as defined in Proposition 5.3 is invariant under the operations from Definition 4.1. The case k≥n−2 is immediate, so assume k=n−3.
Let A1∈𝒜0 and A1⊆A2⊆𝒞. If supp⁡(A2)=supp⁡(A1), then A2∈𝒜0 because |A2|≥|A1|>|supp⁡(A1)|−(n−3). If supp⁡(A2)⊋supp⁡(A1), then
|A2|≥|A1|+1>|supp⁡(A1)|+1−(n−3)≥|supp⁡(A2)|−(n−3)
and so A2∈𝒜0. This implies 𝒜0=↑𝒜0.
Now take A1,A2∈𝒜0 such that A1∩A2≠∅.
If |A1∪A2|≥5, then |(A1∪A2)\{C}|≥4 for all C∈A1∩A2 and so (A1∪A2)\{C}∈𝒜0. Assume now |A1|=|A2|=3 and |A1∪A2|=4. Then |A1∩A2|=2, so A1∩A2∉𝒜0.
Any A∈𝒜0 with |A|=3 has |supp⁡(A)|=n−1 so for any C∈A, supp⁡(A)−{C}=supp⁡(A). Since |A1∩A2|=2 it follows that supp⁡(A1)=supp⁡(A1∩A2)=supp⁡(A2) and hence supp⁡((A1∪A2)\{C})=n−1. This shows that derived dependent sets of cardinality 3 supported on n elements of the ground set of U⁡(n−3,n) cannot be constructed via the operation ϵ. So ϵ(↑𝒜0)=𝒜0.
We conclude that 𝒜=𝒜0.
∎
The bound from Corollary 5.4 is sharp. To see this, take U⁡(n−4,n). Let A1∈𝒜0 and A1⊆A2⊆𝒞. If supp⁡(A2)⊋supp⁡(A1), it is possible that (3) is no longer satisfied, for example, if |A1|=|supp⁡(A1)|−n+5, |A2|=|A1|+1 but |supp⁡(A2)|≥|supp⁡(A1)|+2. Hence, 𝒜1⊋𝒜0.
5.2 Graphical matroids
We will next give an example of the derived matroid of the graphical matroid M⁡(K4). We believe that this may be an illuminating example for future studies of graphical matroids in general, and perhaps even more generally of binary matroids. A key feature of the example is that δ​M​(K4) turns out to have strictly fewer dependent sets than the Longyear derived matroid of M⁡(K4). This foreshadows some of our conjectures in Section 8.

Example 7.4.
Let M be the Vámos matroid as in Example 5.6. Let
A1={a​d​e​f,a​d​g​h,d​e​f​g​h}andA2={a​d​e​f,a​d​g​h,b​c​e​f,b​c​g​h}.
Then A1∈𝒜0 by the nullity condition and it was shown in Example 5.6 that A2∈𝒜1. We now apply operation ϵ (Definition 4.1) on A1 and A2. Since |A1∩A2|=2, A1∩A2∉𝒜1 by Lemma 4.11, and thus S:=(A1∩A2)\{a​d​e​f}∈ϵ⁡(𝒜1). So we get S={a​d​g​h,b​c​e​f,b​c​g​h,d​e​f​g​h} and S∈𝒜.
Let C=a​d​g​h and consider S\{C}: it needs to be either independent or dependent in δ​M. Suppose it is independent, so S\{C}∉𝒜. We have that C−supp⁡(S\{C})=a. Applying Conjecture 7.3 now gives that S∉𝒜, which is a contradiction. Now suppose S\{C}∈𝒜 and let C′=d​e​f​g​h. We have that C′−supp⁡(S\{C,C′})=d. Applying Conjecture 7.3 gives that S\{C,C′}∈𝒜, which is a contradiction since by Lemma 4.11, S\{C,C′} is independent because it has size 2. We conclude that Conjecture 7.3 cannot be true.
Although this example does not disprove Lemma 7.1 for the combinatorial derived matroid, it shows that new ideas are needed in order to prove or disprove the statement.
Unfortunately, we were not able to prove a more precise statement about the independent sets of δ​M. We do have the following straightforward observation about the rank of δ​M.
Lemma 7.5.
Let M be a non-empty connected matroid of rank k. Then the rank of the combinatorial derived matroid δ​M is at most n−k.
Proof.
The nullity of any subset of 𝒞 is at most the nullity of M, which is n−k. This means that any subset of cardinality n−k+1 of 𝒞 is in 𝒜0 and is thus dependent in δ​M. Now the rank of δ​M is the cardinality of its largest independent set, which we just saw is at most n−k.
∎
It is unknown if the rank of the combinatorial derived matroid is always equal to n−k. We give a conjecture and a question towards a solution to this problem.
Conjecture 7.6.
Let M be a matroid such that M∗ has an adjoint. Then δ​M is isomorphic to an adjoint of M∗. In particular, the rank of δ​M is equal to n−k.
It is shown in [14, Lemma 3] that if B is a basis of a representable matroid M and R any representation of M, then the set of fundamental circuits with respect to B is a basis of δO​W​(R). This motivates the following question.
Question 7.7.
Does there always exist a basis B of M such that a subset of the fundamental circuits with respect to B is a basis in δ​M?

8.2 Adjoint
The construction of the combinatorial derived matroid is iterative. If a set of circuits of M satisfies the nullity condition (3) in Definition 4.3, the set is in 𝒜0 hence dependent. If not, the only way to check its (in)dependence is by constructing iteratively all dependent sets of δ​M and see if our set is one of them.
The fact that there are sets for which (in)dependence is hard to check, means it is also difficult to define a closure function of δ​M. We are not optimistic about finding a definition of closure in δ​M without some form of iteration.
As a result of the lack of closure in δ​M, we have not managed to compare the definition of δ​M, that uses dependent sets, to that of the adjoint (Section 3.4), that uses closed sets. We expect the following to be true.
Conjecture 8.7.
If an adjoint of a matroid M exists, one of them is equal to the combinatorial derived matroid of the dual. Moreover, every adjoint of M is less δ​M∗ in the weak order on matroids with ground set 𝒞.
9 Suggestions for further research
We have developed the notion of the combinatorial derived matroid. Contrary to earlier constructions for a derived matroid, our construction exist for all matroids and is unique.
There are many open questions about our construction. Apart from the questions and conjectures already stated in the text, we list here some more ideas for further research.
Question 9.1.
Is there a characterization of the class of matroids N that are isomorphic to the combinatorial derived matroid δ​M of some matroid M?
By Proposition 4.12, a necessary condition is that every element in N that is contained in a circuit is also contained in a circuit of size 3. Many more necessary conditions like this should probably first be obtained, before a complete characterization is feasible.
Question 9.2.
For which matroids does it hold that δ​M=M or δ​M=M∗? The latter property may be more natural, since the rank of δ​M is always equal to the rank of M∗. It is also possible to repeat the procedure of taking the combinatorial derived matroid of the dual multiple times, i.e. study the sequence
M,δ⁡(M∗),δ⁡(δ​(M∗)∗),….
Does this sequence converge? For earlier constructions of the derived matroid, these questions have been studied in [14, Section 3] and [9, Section 4], see also [10].
Question 9.3.
Is there any relation between δ​M and
